turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Imagine finishing a whole quarter with a long list of completed tasks, but your core metrics haven't moved at all. How does a team end up there?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: By fixing whatever feedback is loudest instead of what happens most often. You let one customer writing long emails weigh as much as a hundred people who silently left.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: But feedback pours in from everywhere—support, reviews, sales chats, founder emails. Isn't that stream your task list?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: No, raw feedback is just messages, not problems. To find the real problems, you need to plot those messages on a feedback matrix.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: How do you map that out?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Along two axes. Axis one is what the user was doing—their stage, like sign-up, setting up a first schedule, shift swapping, or payment.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: And axis two?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: What went wrong: didn't find, didn't understand, didn't work, or missing feature. The cell where they intersect gives you a problem statement, like "didn't understand during shift swap."

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: So you can't even categorize a message without reading it to understand what they were trying to do.

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Exactly. And it separates identical words—saying "inconvenient" in payment is a completely different problem with a different cost than "inconvenient" in shift swapping.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: How did this work for Smena, the app for cafe owners and shift workers?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: They had 62 messages in a month. Before categorizing, the most noticeable issue seemed to be a chain owner with six locations who sent four detailed emails about reports.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: But in the matrix, that was just four messages from one single account.

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Right. The real top issue was 21 messages where employees didn't understand if a shift swap was confirmed, and 14 messages from owners looking for spreadsheet import.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: So you have to count unique accounts, not just total messages.

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Always. A cell with 21 messages from 19 accounts means something completely different than 21 messages from 3 accounts.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Are there limitations to relying on this matrix?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: It shows frequency, not importance. Three messages could represent half your revenue, plus it completely misses the silent majority who write nothing and simply leave.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: So it's a tool for sorting what you receive, not a complete picture of every user.

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Exactly. Feedback is raw material, not a task list. A problem only emerges when you group messages by what the person was trying to do, rather than how loudly they wrote.
